issues.legal_issue: A customary right of pre-emption based on vicinage is invalid when it imposes unreasonable restrictions on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a general local custom of pre-emption based on vicinage and had made the required demands.
The claimant owned a house adjacent to the property sold, and the trial court found him entitled to pre-empt under the custom.
The challenged custom restricted both the seller's ability to transfer the property and the purchaser's ability to acquire it, without an advantage to the general public.
issues.conclusion: The customary right of pre-emption based on vicinage was void, and the decree could not be sustained on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 19(1)(f), 19(5), and 13 of the Constitution, the reasoning in Bhau Ram v. B. Baijnath Singh, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 724, that statutory pre-emption based on vicinage imposes unreasonable restrictions on property rights applies equally to a customary right. Such a restriction is not justified by an asserted aim of preventing people of different religions, races, or castes from acquiring property in an area, in light of Article 15. Digambar Singh v. Ahmad Said Khan, L.R. 42 I.A. 10, was referred to concerning the history of pre-emption.

predicates.customary_preemption_claim_based_on_vici: A claimant in a dispute over a property transfer sought pre-emption under a custom based on being a neighbour.
predicates.restricts_seller_and_buyer_property_righ: The custom limited the seller's ability to transfer the property and the buyer's ability to acquire it.
predicates.lacks_general_public_advantage: The restriction did not provide an advantage to the general public.
predicates.customary_vicinage_preemption_is_void: A customary right of pre-emption based on vicinage is invalid.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks pre-emption under a vicinage custom that restricts both the seller and buyer without a general public advantage, the rule treats that customary right as invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A custom or usage having the force of law is included in the laws in force that are subject to fundamental rights protections.
material_facts: The claimant sought to enforce a pre-emption right arising from a custom that the trial court found generally existed in the locality.
The dispute required deciding whether a custom having the force of law was covered by the constitutional provision addressing laws in force.
issues.conclusion: Customs and usages having the force of law are included in the expression laws in force and are subject to Part III of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 13(1) applies to laws in force, and Article 13(3)(a) provides that law includes any custom or usage having the force of law. Article 13(3)(b) inclusively covers laws made before the Constitution even if they were not operating in a particular area or at all; it does not narrow the meaning of law in Article 13(3)(a). Reading custom out of Article 13(1) would leave it unaffected by fundamental rights, although Article 13(2) addresses laws made by the State and custom is not made by the State.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_preexisting_: A party challenged a pre-existing customary rule as inconsistent with fundamental rights.
predicates.custom_or_usage_has_force_of_law: The custom or usage operated as a rule with the force of law.
predicates.custom_or_usage_is_law_in_force_subject_: A custom or usage having the force of law is included among laws in force and is subject to fundamental rights protections.

issues.definition: When a pre-existing custom with the force of law is challenged on fundamental-rights grounds, the rule treats it as a law in force subject to those protections.
